ami_style_notes: The meeting has mostly short-to-medium turns, with a relaxed, friendly pre-meeting chat followed by long, presentation-style monologues and medium-length technical Q&A exchanges. Overlap and interruptions are light but frequent in the form of quick acknowledgments, repeated “yeah”s, greetings, and brief interjections; speakers generally let answers run rather than cutting in. The tone is informal and collegial despite specialized language, using fillers and disfluencies heavily (“um,” “uh,” “you know,” restarts, repetitions, self-corrections). Participants hedge often with phrases like “I think,” “sort of,” “maybe,” “it seems,” and “I guess,” especially when speculating. Questions are usually prefaced politely—“I have a question,” “can I ask,” “naive question”—then unfold in multipart, exploratory form. Disagreement is indirect: people frame alternatives as open questions or uncertainty rather than blunt contradiction, and build on prior remarks with praise, clarification, or extensions. Introductions and transitions are somewhat formal, but the surrounding conversation remains warm, spontaneous, and lightly joking.
research_problem: Understanding how urban green space affects mental health outcomes in low-income communities

speakers.name: Dr. Anika Raman
speakers.background: A cognitive-affective neuroscientist with 12 years of experience studying chronic stress, environmental contexts, and allostatic load in community-based cohorts. She has led longitudinal studies combining ecological momentary assessment, salivary cortisol, heart-rate variability, actigraphy, GPS traces, and wearable electrodermal activity. As project manager, she is responsible for aligning the survey schedule, wearable protocol, biospecimen logistics, and cross-site quality assurance.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Frames park effects as potentially operating through time-varying exposure to restorative and threat-reducing environmental cues: time spent in vegetated settings, visual contact with greenery during daily travel, ambient heat and noise reduction, social co-presence, and opportunities for physical activity. She wants the conceptual model to distinguish proximal stress-regulation processes from downstream self-reported mental-health outcomes, and argues for repeated within-person measures that can capture acute autonomic and affective responses rather than relying solely on residential proximity. She is likely to press for a pre-specified mechanistic pathway linking exposure, hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis regulation, sympathetic arousal, perceived safety, and depressive or anxiety symptoms.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: highly confident in their discipline's contribution

speakers.name: Dr. Marisol Vega
speakers.background: A comparative urban political scientist with 15 years of research on municipal governance, participatory planning, policing, and racialized neighborhood investment in U.S. cities. Her work combines policy-process tracing, archival analysis of capital budgets and planning documents, interviews with residents and local officials, meeting observation, and geocoded administrative data on service provision and enforcement. She has partnered with tenant organizations and park advisory councils in several of the proposed study cities.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Treats parks not as neutral amenities but as politically produced institutions whose benefits depend on governance, maintenance, rules of use, policing practices, and residents' capacity to shape implementation. She will caution that nominal proximity can coexist with constrained access when surveillance, exclusionary design, fears of harassment, or uneven programming make a space unusable for particular groups. She wants the study to measure participatory institutions, distributive decision-making, implementation fidelity, and the sequence through which park investment may also accompany rezoning, speculative development, or intensified enforcement. Her contribution emphasizes that community power and perceived legitimacy are plausible determinants of whether a green-space intervention becomes health-promoting or contributes to insecurity and displacement.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: highly confident in their discipline's contribution

speakers.name: Daniel Okafor
speakers.background: A fifth-year economics PhD student specializing in urban, public, and health economics. He has built quasi-experimental panels using parcel records, residential address histories, property transactions, eviction filings, municipal capital-improvement data, and survey linkages. His dissertation uses event-study and difference-in-differences designs to estimate the distributional consequences of transit and neighborhood infrastructure investments, with particular attention to migration, treatment timing, spillovers, and selective attrition.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Defines the central problem as identifying the causal effect of exposure to park investment or changing neighborhood greenness, rather than conflating it with preexisting differences between residents who live near parks and those who do not. He will push for a transparent treatment definition based on funding, opening, renovation completion, and spatial catchments; an event-time design with staggered-adoption-robust estimators; and explicit analyses of residential sorting, displacement, compositional change, and concurrent investments. He favors preregistering primary estimands, comparison areas, buffer specifications, migration rules, and sensitivity analyses. While dominant on identification and data architecture, he defers to neuroscience on the validity and timing of stress measures and to political science on how governance and local implementation should be operationalized as moderators or mechanisms.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: defers to other experts outside their domain

benchmark_task: Given a meeting transcript where the same term was used by two different researchers from two different disciplines, test that the AI identifies the term as having two different meanings with definitions according to each discipline.

seed_spec.benchmark_task: Given a meeting transcript where the same term was used by two different researchers from two different disciplines, test that the AI identifies the term as having two different meanings with definitions according to each discipline.
seed_spec.explicit_instruction: Embed the term "exposure" naturally in the discussion, used by both the neuroscientist and the economist without either speaker noting that they mean different things. The neuroscientist should use "exposure" to mean an individual's direct, time-varying contact with green environments, such as time spent in or visually encountering vegetation, which may influence stress physiology and neural or psychological processes. The economist should use "exposure" to mean assignment or treatment intensity generated by a policy or environmental change, such as residence within a defined catchment of a newly funded park or a measured change in neighborhood greenness used in a causal design. Let the political scientist complicate the conversation by raising unequal access, policing, resident participation, or governance, but do not have anyone explicitly flag the terminological mismatch. The ambiguity should arise organically while the team discusses study design, measurement, and causal inference.

meanings.definition: An individual's direct and often time-varying contact with green space or green sensory cues, such as time spent in a park, walking under tree cover, or visual exposure to vegetation. It is treated as a proximal experience that may affect stress, affect, cognition, or physiological and neural processes.

A treatment, assignment, or dose variable defined by policy-relevant eligibility, geographic proximity, residence, or a change in environmental conditions, used to estimate the causal effect of green-space provision or access. It need not imply that a resident actually spent time in or perceptually encountered the green space.

ground_truth.key_distinction: The neuroscientific use refers to experienced individual contact and a putative mechanism, whereas the economic use refers to analytically defined treatment status or intensity for causal identification.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marisol Vega
transcript.text: Hi, everyone—can you all hear me on the backup link? Great. I know we only have the room until 4:30, so maybe we can get moving: I’d really like us to leave today with a model where the park isn’t just a distance-based exposure, but something whose actual availability is shaped by maintenance, rules, enforcement, and community voice. Then we can be pretty disciplined about what has to go into the preregistration versus what we trace alongside the main analysis.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Anika Raman
transcript.text: Yeah, exactly—and for me “availability” has to become actual time-varying encounter. I’d preregister exposure as GPS-linked minutes in or alongside vegetated space, canopy and visual-green contact during travel, with windows preceding EMA affect, EDA/HRV, and cortisol; residential distance can be an assignment-relevant measure—

transcript.speaker: Daniel Okafor
transcript.text: —but I really don’t think GPS minutes can be the primary exposure. They’re post-investment behavior and they’re jointly determined by baseline health, work, safety, and who remains in the corridor. Primary has to be a pre-specified, assignment-style exposure: project timing and intensity within fixed catchments, then use encounter as a mechanism outcome.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Anika Raman
transcript.text: —right, primary estimand, yes. I’m not trying to make GPS minutes the treatment; I’m saying the pathway has to be preregistered too, with lagged encounter predicting the acute physiology and EMA before we ever ask whether symptoms move.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marisol Vega
transcript.text: Yes—and the fixed catchment treatment needs an implementation regime attached to it. A renovation completed on the same date can mean very different things if, say, programming is sparse, maintenance is deferred, or enforcement ramps up, so I’d code a small set of preregistered corridor-level conditions—participatory capacity, maintenance, programming, and enforcement—and treat GPS encounter as one downstream indicator of whether the public institution became usable.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Anika Raman
transcript.text: Yeah, and that gives us a clean mediation sequence rather than treating use as evidence of effect by itself. For the wearable arm, I’d specify that implementation conditions predict encounter and perceived safety/restoration, then test whether encounter in, say, the preceding two-to-six-hour window is associated with lower sympathetic arousal and better vagal indices before the next EMA affect report.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marisol Vega
transcript.text: And I’d be careful about the direction there: perceived safety isn’t only a mediator of encounter. It may be directly altered by patrol patterns, cameras, or hostile-use rules, and those can raise arousal even for residents who never enter the park. So maybe our corridor condition coding has a pre-specified enforcement and governance component, with the richer process tracing—who decided what, and when—running in parallel.

transcript.speaker: Daniel Okafor
transcript.text: Yeah, I think that works if those conditions are coded at a defensible pre-outcome date and we distinguish ones that precede implementation from things the investment itself changes. For the main design, I’d interact the assignment-style exposure with a small, frozen set of baseline governance and enforcement measures; then the evolving conditions, perceived safety, and GPS encounter can sit in the pathway analysis without contaminating the treatment definition.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marisol Vega
transcript.text: Yeah, that distinction is workable. I can freeze baseline measures from the year before each completion—whether there was an active advisory body, documented resident input with any formal uptake, maintenance and programming commitments, and the enforcement regime—then separately code post-completion changes. The tricky bit is that “baseline” enforcement may already be responding to anticipated redevelopment, so the archive timeline should flag that rather than pretending it’s exogenous.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Anika Raman
transcript.text: Yeah, and for the wearable analysis we can carry that flag explicitly rather than bury it: anticipated-redevelopment enforcement becomes a corridor-level time marker and a sensitivity stratum. The acute models still need the actual temporal ordering—green encounter first, then safety/restoration and autonomic response—otherwise we’ll be attributing a patrol-related EDA spike to the park itself.

transcript.speaker: Daniel Okafor
transcript.text: Right, and I’d put that anticipation marker directly into the event-time calendar, not just the wearable models. We should separate announcement, construction start, reopening, and completion, because if enforcement or moves begin at announcement, a completion-only coefficient is averaging several different treatments. Then the administrative file lets us show whether the apparent pretrend is actually selective exit or turnover.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Anika Raman
transcript.text: Yes. And on the wearable side, those dates let us define clean exclusion or sensitivity windows around construction and announcement, because noise, disrupted routes, and acute uncertainty can move HRV and EDA independently of green contact. I’d also want the event-time file aligned to each participant’s actual wear days, not just the survey waves, or we lose the temporal resolution that makes the mechanism piece credible.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marisol Vega
transcript.text: Yes, and I can build that event-time calendar from the archive rather than treating announcement as a single date. We should distinguish a public announcement from the first observable governance change—like an MOU, zoning action, capital appropriation, or patrol directive—because in a couple of the corridors those were months apart. I can make a feasible coded chronology for every site now, then reserve the finer process tracing for the cases where the estimates look especially sensitive.

transcript.speaker: Daniel Okafor
transcript.text: That chronology is exactly what we need. Could you also give each date a source-confidence flag and distinguish citywide policy shifts from corridor-specific actions? Then we can prespecify which dates enter the treatment calendar, use the uncertain ones in sensitivity analyses, and avoid silently coding a broad policing change as though it were caused by one park project.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marisol Vega
transcript.text: Yes, I can do that. I’ll use a corridor-specific versus citywide tag, a source hierarchy—formal directive or appropriation versus minutes or press reporting—and an uncertainty flag; the one thing I’d preserve is that citywide shifts can still be politically consequential if their local implementation was concentrated in these corridors. So I’ll code the policy’s scope separately from evidence of corridor-level deployment.

transcript.speaker: Daniel Okafor
transcript.text: Yeah, that separation is important. For identification I’d treat citywide shifts as common shocks unless the deployment measure varies at the corridor-by-time level; otherwise they belong in the calendar and controls, not as part of a given park’s treatment. And where deployment does concentrate locally, we should probably call it a concurrent intervention and estimate sensitivity bounds rather than fold it into greenness exposure.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marisol Vega
transcript.text: Yeah, and the sensitivity bounds should not erase the institutional mechanism. If a locally concentrated patrol directive is concurrent, I can code whether it was framed as park stewardship, disorder enforcement, or something else, because those imply pretty different effects on practical access and legitimacy even if we keep it analytically separate from the park treatment.

transcript.speaker: Daniel Okafor
transcript.text: Right, and that framing can be in the mechanism appendix even if the primary estimand holds it apart. I’d just want a hard rule in the preregistration: when a patrol or redevelopment action is sufficiently co-timed and localized that we can’t construct a credible comparison, we flag that site-event as bundled treatment rather than interpreting its coefficient as a park-only effect.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Marisol Vega
transcript.text: Yes, that rule makes sense. I’ll build the chronology so bundled site-events are visibly classified rather than absorbed into a residual category, and I can add a short qualitative note on the governing rationale and local deployment evidence. That leaves us able to say where we have a park-opening estimand versus where we really have a corridor transformation.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Anika Raman
transcript.text: Yeah, and for the bundled events I’d keep the acute wearable inference explicitly descriptive or stratified, not try to force a park-specific physiological pathway there. We can still ask whether green encounter precedes lower arousal within people on valid wear days, but label that as mechanism-pattern evidence under a corridor transformation rather than mediation of a clean park effect.

transcript.speaker: Daniel Okafor
transcript.text: Yeah. Then I think the preregistration needs an explicit estimand table: clean, unbundled completions get the staggered event-study as primary; bundled corridor transformations are a separately labeled exposure class, with no park-only causal interpretation. We should also lock the migration rule there—intent-to-treat by baseline address, plus a residential-history sensitivity—before we look at who leaves after announcement.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Anika Raman
transcript.text: Yeah, and the baseline-address ITT is compatible with the wearable piece as long as we don’t quietly treat post-move GPS exposure as though it reflects the assigned corridor. I’d retain those wear days for the within-person encounter-to-arousal analyses, but tag address status and make the mover restriction a prespecified sensitivity; otherwise selective exit will get mixed into both adherence and exposure.

transcript.speaker: Daniel Okafor
transcript.text: Yeah, exactly. For the primary panel, baseline address assignment stays fixed even after a move, and then we report address-history exposure as a sensitivity rather than conditioning the sample on staying. I’ll draft the estimand table with that rule, the bundled-event classification, and the event-date hierarchy so we have something concrete to mark up before the 18th.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Anika Raman
transcript.text: And I’ll put a parallel wearable QC box into that table: valid-day thresholds for HRV, EDA, GPS, and EMA linkage, plus site-level adherence reporting. Lakeview’s gap can’t become an invisible exclusion mechanism, so we should freeze a realistic minimum wear-time rule now and flag any site-specific missingness in the mechanism estimates.

transcript.speaker: Daniel Okafor
transcript.text: Yeah, agreed—freeze the QC rules and report Lakeview missingness by site and event time.

realism_signals: interruptions, cut-off sentences, or people jumping in
issues: Naturalness is the principal weakness: nearly every turn is a polished, fully formed technical paragraph that states a position, qualifies it, and lands on a concrete design implication. Examples include turns 8, 13, 16, 18, and 21. This reads more like an edited methods workshop transcript than spontaneous speech.

The few disfluencies are largely superficial turn-openers or punctuation-style interruptions (for example, turns 2-4 and repeated opening 'Yeah' in turns 6, 8-12, 15-25) rather than speech that genuinely searches for phrasing. The dialogue needs more mid-thought revisions, incomplete points, backchannels, and occasional uncertainty.

Turn lengths and rhetorical structure are unusually uniform. Even the short turn 25 is a clean approval plus action directive, while most other turns are similarly dense 50-80-word interventions. Add some brief acknowledgments, clarifying questions, and partially developed contributions.

Daniel's persona is somewhat less distinct than intended: despite being the nominal dominant speaker, he is highly accommodating and repeatedly uses the same 'Yeah, ...' agreement structure in turns 8, 11, 14, 16, 18, 21, 23, and 25. More characteristic econometric shorthand, selective questioning, or sharper prioritization would distinguish him further without making him adversarial.

The meeting has only a minimal concrete contextual anchor: Lakeview appears once in turns 24-25. Adding a little ordinary meeting texture or site-specific context earlier would make the setting feel less purely on-agenda.

The seed itself is well embedded and recoverable: Raman's direct, time-varying sensory/behavioral contact is clear in turns 2, 4, 6, 10, 12, 20, and 22, while Okafor's assignment-style/catchment treatment meaning is clear in turns 3, 8, 16, 21, and 23. No participant explicitly identifies the terminological mismatch.
